schools.summary: Gill weighs whether the 'heathen' are the Jews or (as he decides, with Acts 4:25) the Gentiles, 'rage' being a tumultuous mob-gathering; Calvin sets David in the foreground as literal subject and type, his shadow-kingdom yielding a prophecy 'truly predicted concerning' Christ, not merely allegorized.

Keil and Delitzsch read a four-voice prophetic drama whose middle speaker, the Anointed, is not the poet; Ellicott renders 'why did the nations band together or muster' (the verb a hapax) and 'imagine' as 'mutter,' letting the reference range from a historical prince to a higher Messianic fulfilment.

Clarke supposes David wrote it after taking Jerusalem and routing the Philistine confederacy, David typifying Christ; Wesley glosses the 'heathen' of those who raged against David (2 Samuel 5) and against Christ (Acts 4:25).
Henry hears one great struggle over Christ's kingdom, hell and heaven contesting it, the opposition spiteful, deliberate, resolute, and confederate.
Augustine takes the psalm wholly of Christ: the 'why' means 'in vain,' for the persecutors did not accomplish the destruction they wished.

debates.question: Does the psalm speak directly of Christ, or first of David literally as the type of Christ?

sides.position: chiefly and directly of Christ and his persecutors
of David literally, as the type whose shadow-kingdom was truly fulfilled in Christ (typico-literal)

themes: the four-voice drama of the psalm

schools.summary: Ellicott reads 'set themselves' as hostile array (cf. Jeremiah 46:4), 'take counsel' as 'mustering to carry out their plans,' and dates the distinctive Messianic sense of 'anointed' to this psalm; Keil and Delitzsch place Jahve enthroned, his 'futures' describing continual, unhindered control.
Gill names the kings — Herod the Great, Herod Antipas, Pilate, and all since who persecute Christ in his members.
Wesley reads 'of the earth' as contempt for their madness against the God of heaven; Clarke adds the Chaldee 'against his Messiah,' the title referring first to David, then to Christ.
Henry: the war is against all religion and Christianity in particular, for enemies of Christ are enemies of God — 'they have hated both me and my Father.'

themes: against the LORD and his anointed

schools.summary: Wesley reads the second clause as the same defiance with more emphasis, flinging the cords far away; Clarke (citing Bishop Horne) finds the ground of opposition in rebellious nature's refusal of divine restraint — 'the Church may be tolerated if she will give up her discipline.'
Gill fixes whose words these are — not the saints throwing off Jewish ceremonies, but the heathen and their kings against the Lord and his Anointed.
Ellicott marks the poem's movement from whispered plot to loud menace, and the Septuagint/Vulgate 'yoke' for 'cords' (a restive animal, cf. Isaiah 10:27).
Augustine: the rebels' aim is that the Christian religion not bind them nor be imposed upon them.
Henry: children of Belial who cannot endure the yoke — yet the bands are 'cords of a man' and 'bands of love,' the cords of conscience and God's commandments they cast away.

themes: cords of a man, bands of love

schools.summary: Gill sets God's serene 'sitting' against the heathen's running to and fro, the laughter an anthropopathy showing how vain their attempts must be.

Clarke has God contemn their puny efforts and confound their devices; Wesley reads the heavenly throne as proof of his certain knowledge and irresistible power, his laughter a despising of their crafty devices.
Ellicott calls the turn a Hebrew sublimity that ascribes to God the very 'irony of events' he controls.
Henry: God sits still and vanquishes them, the perfect repose of the Eternal Mind a comfort under our own disquiet.
Augustine forbids reading the laughter carnally, of cheek or nostril: it is the power God gives his saints to foreknow that Christ's rule shall possess all nations, exposing the rebels' 'vain thing.'

outliers.note: Reads God's 'laughter' and 'derision' not of any divine emotion but as the power of foreknowledge granted to the saints, by which they see that Christ's name shall pervade all nations and the rebels 'meditate a vain thing.'

themes: he that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh
the repose of the Eternal Mind

schools.summary: Gill takes the 'speaking' as God's providences, not his word, and in wrath not love — referring it chiefly to the destruction of Jerusalem after the Gospel had advanced among the Gentiles.
Clarke widens it to the ruin of the unbelieving Jews by Rome and the fall of the opposing emperors, until the empire came under Constantine, whom God converted.

Ellicott hears 'then' as a thunder-roll climax and renders 'vex' as intensively terrify ('in his nostrils and in his heat'); Keil and Delitzsch liken the verse to a peal of thunder and 'sore displeasure' to the lightning's flash, closing the strophe with Jahve's own words.
Henry: God despises the rebels yet is justly provoked — the breath of his mouth their confusion; a word made us, a word can unmake us, and setting up his Son's kingdom is their greatest vexation.

themes: speak unto them in his wrath

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the pronoun emphatic and lays out the rendering of the verb — literally 'poured out' (molten metal, cf. Isaiah 40:19), hence 'set up,' though Gesenius/Ewald/Symmachus read 'anointed'; Keil and Delitzsch rule for 'set firmly' (so LXX, Jerome, Luther), the prince 'installed' not 'anointed.'
Gill reads Zion as the church of God under the Gospel — loved, chosen, fortified, immovable on Christ the Rock, holy through God's presence and Spirit.
Wesley: 'my king' rules in God's stead for his glory; Zion is first the city of David, then Jerusalem, the temple, and the church, Jewish and Christian.
Henry: as David won Zion's stronghold, so Christ is exalted and fixed at the Father's right hand — 'I have set him, I have settled him' — his throne set up in believers' hearts.

debates.question: Does the verb rendered 'set' mean 'established/installed' or 'anointed'?

sides.position: poured out firm, hence 'set up / installed' (so the ancient versions)
'anointed,' agreeing with the mention of the Messiah
holders: Gesenius and Ewald (as reported by Ellicott)

themes: yet have I set my king

schools.summary: Gill assigns 'I will declare the decree' to the Anointed King, the decree being God's saving purpose (what precedes), while the sonship is not from any decree but 'from his nature.'

Henry roots the kingdom in an eternal decree, the federal transaction of Father and Son, and reads 'begotten' of both the eternal generation (Hebrews 1:5) and its demonstration by the resurrection (Acts 13:33).

Clarke denies that 'today' can express eternity, taking 'begotten' as 'manifested' — declared Son of God by the resurrection (Romans 1:4); Wesley holds both senses but leans to the manifestation in time.

Ellicott sets the words on a coronation-day, the 'new birthday' of the monarch, the engraved 'decree' a formal ordinance, the thought ranging on to the Messianic fulfilment claimed by tradition (Hebrews 5:5; 2 Samuel 7:14).

debates.question: What does 'this day have I begotten thee' denote?

sides.position: the eternal generation of the Son (Henry adds: and its demonstration by the resurrection)
not eternity but the Son's manifestation/declaration in time by the resurrection
the historical coronation-day of the anointed king, ranging on to a Messianic fulfilment

themes: this day have I begotten thee

schools.summary: Gill hears in 'ask' no inferiority but Father-Son intimacy: as Christ asked for the elect in the covenant of grace and was not denied, so here the asking is answered in a world-wide dominion.
Clarke reads the second branch of Christ's office — the risen Mediator's intercession, receiving the nations and sending his apostles to preach to every man.
Henry frames a title by agreement: the Son asks, taking the human nature, and receives universal dominion — the Gentiles too, awaiting the kingdoms becoming Christ's (Revelation 11:15).
Keil and Delitzsch read ahead to the poet's application: the 'judges of the earth' are its rulers throughout its breadth, addressed in the light of what the seer has beheld.
Gill directs the rod not at the Gentile inheritance but at the rebellious, and reconciles the Septuagint 'rule/feed them' with 'break' — justice without mercy comes to the same.

Ellicott sets out the rod as shepherd's crook (LXX 'pasture,' Leviticus 27:32), sceptre (Psalms 125:3), or rod of correction (Proverbs 22:15), judging the 'dashing in pieces' to fix the last sense (Milton's iron sceptre).
Clarke refers the iron rod to the Jewish nation ruined by Rome for unbelief; Wesley extends it to the fall of the Pagan power, complete only when all opposing principality is put down.
Henry ties it to the iron kingdom of Daniel 2:40 and the potter's vessel of Revelation 2:27: 'thou shalt do it,' and effectually — nations ruined rather than the church unbuilt.

themes: on Jerusalem, Rome, or all opposing power
the golden and the iron sceptre

schools.summary: Gill extends the address to kings under the Gospel and their subjects — great men are not always wise, and to rise against the Messiah is folly, for there is no counsel against the Lord.
Clarke widens it to all rulers, reading 'be instructed' as 'be reformed' — cast away idolatrous maxims and receive the Gospel as the basis of the law.
Henry: he who could destroy takes no pleasure in it but puts them in the way to be happy; kings must receive law from Christ, standing level with the meanest subject.

Keil and Delitzsch read 'now therefore' as a practical conclusion to kings in general, bidding them show discernment and be admonished; Ellicott opens the psalm's fourth section and recalls 'et nunc reges intelligite' on the medal struck after the execution of Charles I.

themes: counsel offered in place of the rod

schools.summary: Gill: the service is to the true Jehovah alone, not the idols of the Gentiles; kings need not lay aside their crowns but serve God in their office according to his will.

Clarke joins reverence to happiness, a filial fear moderating joy before the judgment-seat; Wesley reads fear as an awful sense of majesty and the trembling as a guard against turning grace into wantonness.

Henry holds fear and joy consistent — God feared as holy, rejoiced in as benefactor; salvation wrought with fear and trembling (Philippians 2:12), rejoicing as though we rejoiced not (1 Corinthians 7:30).
Ellicott fixes 'rejoice with trembling' as literally 'quake,' used of both joy and terror, which the old versions softened ('pray,' 'cleave,' 'praise') where the AV keeps the trembling.
Gill retains 'Kiss the Son' (of v.7), the word from a root to choose and purify — God's elect and pure One — the kiss rendering love, homage, and adoration.

Wesley keeps 'kiss the Son of God' in token of subjection, the least of his anger terrible; Clarke leans to the versions — 'bar' a Chaldee word, the sense 'embrace that which is pure, the doctrine of God.'

Ellicott holds 'Kiss the Son' 'must be surrendered' — the ancient versions and the Aramaic 'bar' (vs. native 'ben' in v.7) against it — rendering 'proffer pure homage' to Jehovah, with Rabbinical and modern authority; 'find their refuge' for 'put their trust.'

Henry keeps 'Kiss the Son' as reconciliation, worship, affection, and allegiance to Christ, 'lest he be angry' (the Father's wrath abiding, John 3:36) and 'lest ye perish from the way' — hell from the way to heaven.

debates.question: Should 'Kiss the Son' (bar = the Son) be retained, or surrendered for 'do homage / embrace discipline'?

sides.position: retain 'Kiss the Son' — the Son of God, Christ
surrender it — 'bar' is Aramaic and the versions read 'discipline'; render 'proffer pure homage' or 'embrace what is pure'

themes: blessed are all they that trust
